10.1016/s0168-8278(26)01051-2.title: SAT-368-YI ALNE 2.0: a histopathology-based deep learning model accurately discriminates autoimmune hepatitis and primary biliary cholangitis and helps identify the dominant phenotype in variant cases
10.1016/s0168-8278(26)01051-2.abstract: Background and aims: Differentiating autoimmune hepatitis (AIH), from primary biliary cholangitis (PBC), and their variant syndrome (VS) is challenging due to overlapping histological and clinical features. The ALNE deep learning (DL) model has shown promise in AIH–PBC discrimination but has not been validated in large cohorts or applied to VS. We aimed to develop and externally validate a histopathology-based DL model for discriminating AIH, PBC, and characterizing VS using a large, ethnically diverse, multicenter cohort. Method: We conducted a multicenter study including a training cohort of 1216 patients with AIH (n = 900, mean age at diagnosis 53 ± 16 years, 66% female) and PBC (n = 316, mean age at diagnosis 52 ± 11 years, 73% female). Digitized liver biopsy slides and clinical data were collected from 21 international centers across Europe, Asia, North and South America and processed using the UNI2 foundation model to extract histopathological features. ALNE 2.0, a binary classification model (AIH vs. PBC), was developed using 5-fold cross-validation and externally validated on 207 patients (AIH n = 162, mean age at diagnosis 53 ± 17 years, 67% female; PBC n = 45, 52 ± 9 years, 91% female) from two additional centers. The model was then applied to 198 VS cases from 17 countries (mean age at diagnosis 51 ± 14 years, 53% female), generating a probability score. Logistic and linear regression analyses examined clinical variables associated with AIH vs PBC classification probabilities. Results: In 5-fold cross-validation (training cohort: AIH n = 900, PBC n = 316), ALNE 2.0 achieved a mean AUROC of 0.92 (95% CI 0.88–0.96), with average precision of 0.97 (95% CI 0.96–0.99) for AIH and 0.79 (95% CI 0.68–0.91) for PBC. In independent external validation (AIH n = 162, PBC n = 45), performance remained high: AUROC of 0.94, average precision of 0.98 for AIH and 0.83 for PBC. In VS cases (n = 198), predictions were evenly distributed (AIH 46.5%, PBC 53.5%), with probabilities polarizing toward AIH or PBC phenotypes rather than intermediate values. Cases classified as AIH had significantly higher alanine aminotransferase levels (OR 1.18, 95% CI 1.02–1.38, p = 0.031) at presentation, while those classified as PBC more frequently exhibited GP210 antibody positivity (coeff. −0.154, 95% CI −0.305 to −0.004, p = 0.045). Conclusion: ALNE 2.0 accurately discriminates AIH and PBC in a large, ethnically diverse multicenter cohort and provides quantitative assessment of the dominant disease phenotype in VS cases.

10.1016/s0168-8278(26)01056-1.title: SAT-377 AI-driven proteomic profiling differentiates composite improvement following treatment with nebokitug in PSC
10.1016/s0168-8278(26)01056-1.abstract: Background and aims: Primary sclerosing cholangitis (PSC) is a chronic liver disease, characterized by persistent and progressive inflammation and fibrosis. The phase 2 SPRING study of nebokitug, an anti-CCL24-monoclonal antibody, showed anti-inflammatory, antifibrotic, and anti-cholestatic activity in PSC patients. We present a machine-learning model trained on treatment-associated proteomic changes to characterize nebokitug’s impact on the liver. In addition, integration with a liver-specific atlas proteome allows evaluation of coordinated liver-derived protein changes following treatment. Method: Serum protein levels in patients with PSC were quantified by Olink explore HT, before and after 15 weeks treatment with nebokitug (10 mg/kg; n = 21, 20 mg/kg; n = 27). All measured proteins were used to model a composite improvement outcome requiring reductions in ELF score, transient elastography, and PROC3, using penalized logistic regression (Elastic Net). Feature importance was aggregated from 500 iterations of repeated 5-fold crossvalidation. Consensus was defined by features selected in ≥50% of iterations. Model performance was evaluated via AUROC and validated using permutation testing. Pathway and network analyses were performed on contributing proteins. PCA was performed on sub-groups of proteins shown to be liver specific. Results: The model accurately differentiated patients who met the composite improvement criterion from those who did not, achieving a mean AUROC of 0.92 in repeated cross-validation. Permutation testing confirmed the model’s validity, outperforming random noise models (mean null AUROC 0.59; p < 0.05). Stability analysis resulted in a protein signature consistently selected across iterations. Pathway analysis showed metabolic, catabolic and extracellular matrix related pathways, predominantly expressed in the liver. Analysis of baselineto-week 15 changes using a liver-specific atlas proteome allowed clear discrimination between the groups, as shown by PCA. Conclusion: AI work based on proteomics was successful in distinguishing a composite efficacy improvement outcome to treatment with nebokitug in patients with PSC. Patients who meet the criteria showed differential expressions of liver proteins, with functional liver related proteins as the main drivers of this change. This analysis highlights treatment-associated improvement following nebokitug therapy, as well as the importance of CCL24 blockade in liver diseases and PSC pathology.

10.1016/s0168-8278(26)00364-8.title: OS-054 A confidence-aware artificial intelligence pathology model for cholangiocarcinoma diagnosis
10.1016/s0168-8278(26)00364-8.abstract: Background and aims: Intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma (ICCA) is a highly lethal primary liver cancer. Histologically, ICCA is difficult to diagnose as its morphological and immunohistochemical features significantly overlap with those of metastatic adenocarcinomas. This leads to additional workup and treatment delays. We aimed to develop and prospectively validate a clinically oriented artificial intelligence (AI) model that differentiates ICCA from metastatic cancers on routine liver biopsy whole-slide images (WSIs) and provides case-level confidence estimates. Method: The retrospective cohort comprised 544 adults with ICCA (n = 281) or liver metastases (n = 263) from five European liver centres, split into training and internal test sets. The model was obtained by applying pathology foundation models and training the slide-level aggregators. To quantify prediction confidence, an out-of-distribution detection module (G-ODIN) was added and case-level confidence scores were derived from predictive entropy (PE). Diagnostic performance was assessed by area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) and false positive rate (FPR). PE distributions were compared using Mann–Whitney U tests. The model was further prospectively validated in two independent cohorts from France (Avicenne and Reims University Hospitals) and Asia (Rela Institute, India and Yonsei University of Medicine, South Korea). Results: On the internal test set, the model achieved an AUC of 0.86 and an FPR of 0.19 (best performance using CONCH/TITAN). After addition of the G-ODIN module, we observed that PE was lower in correctly classified cases vs misclassified cases, confirming that it could be used as a confidence metric ( p = 0.003). After PE thresholding (threshold of 0.54), AUC reached 0.944 with an FPR of 0. The model was further prospectively validated using the PE threshold. In the French prospective cohort (n = 25), all samples were correctly classified (AUC of 1, 32% of patients could be predicted according to PE thresholding). In the Asian cohort (n = 136), all but one patient were correctly classified (AUC of 0.965, 23.5% of patients could be predicted according to PE thresholding). Conclusion: We developed and prospectively validated a confidencebased artificial intelligence model to assist the differential diagnosis between ICCA and liver metastases on routine liver biopsies. Our approach may help reduce unnecessary investigations and treatment delays for patients with suspected ICCA.

10.1016/s0168-8278(26)00410-1.title: OS-099 AI-powered cell-free DNA methylation profiling for identification of treatment-eligible MASLD patients: a multi-cohort validation study
10.1016/s0168-8278(26)00410-1.abstract: Background and aims: With the approval of resmetirom and semaglutide for the treatment of MASH with moderate-to-advanced fibrosis (F2-F3), accurate identification of treatment-eligible patients has become a critical clinical need. Current non-invasive tests (NITs) result in missing almost a third of the treatment-eligible patients as they were predominantly developed for detecting advanced fibrosis (F3-F4). We developed and validated an AI-powered cell-free DNA (cfDNA) methylation platform optimized for detecting MASH with F2-F3 to address this diagnostic gap. Method: This multi-cohort study includes 553 biopsy-confirmed MASLD patients from 3 independent cohorts across the US and Europe: (1) Duke MASLD Biobank (n = 276), (2) University Medical Center Mainz Biobank (n = 73), and (3) Akero Therapeutics’ SYNCHRONY Phase 3 screening population (n = 204). Deep methylation sequencing of plasma cfDNA was performed, generating 112 terabytes of genomic data. A novel transformer architecture (LiquidTransformer 89 million parameters), trained on a 20,000 core cluster, was developed to identify clinically significant fibrosis. Test performance was evaluated for the detection of: (1) significant fibrosis (F2-F3) in non-cirrhotic patients and (2) cirrhosis (F4). Performance was compared head-to-head against Fib4, VCTE and ELF on matched samples. All performance results were measured on the validation set. Results: For detection of treatment-eligible fibrosis, F2-F3, and cirrhosis detection the test achieved AUC of 0.83 and 0.80 respectively. In direct comparison on matched subsets of samples, cfDNA methylation test outperformed Fib4 (AUC 0.82 vs 0.71) across all datasets with delta AUC 0.07, 0.07 and 0.13 for Duke, Mainz and Akero respectively. On a subset of Akero samples n = 201 where other comparators were available the test (AUC = 0.82) outperformed ELF (AUC = 0.69), VCTE (AUC = 0.67) and Fib4 (AUC = 0.64). Notably, the Akero cohort represents a clinically pre-selected population yet the model maintained robust performance. Performance was consistent across sex and diabetes status. Conclusion: This AI-powered cfDNA methylation platform accurately identifies MASLD patients eligible for treatment while excluding cirrhosis, directly addressing a diagnostic gap in current guidelinerecommended NIT pathways. The technology demonstrates consistent performance across independent international cohorts including a clinical trial screening population, uniquely positioning it to be considered for integration into treatment decision algorithms.

10.1016/s0168-8278(26)01637-5.title: WED-085 Deep learning integration of nuclear magnetic resonance metabolomics and NASH-FibroTest biomarkers improves bloodbased prediction of liver fat measured by magnetic resonance imaging
10.1016/s0168-8278(26)01637-5.abstract: Background and aims: Magnetic resonance imaging proton density fat fraction (MRI-PDFF) is the reference for quantifying hepatic steatosis but is not suitable for large scale screening or longitudinal follow up. Nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) metabolomics captures lipid signatures associated with hepatic fat accumulation, while Nash-FibroTest (NFT) biomarkers reflect liver injuries and metabolic dysfunction. We aimed to assess whether deep learning models combining NMR and available NFT biomarkers improve discrimination of PDFF-defined steatosis stages. Method: Participants from the UK Biobank with available PDFF, NMR, and a subset of NFT markers (SteatoTest-2-proxy: ALT and AST transaminases, gamma-glutamyltranspeptidase, apolipoproteinA1, triglycerides, cholesterol, glycated hemoglobin, age, sex with R2 = 0.91[%95 CI 0.88–0.92] vs original SteatoTest-2, n = 307) were included. High dimensional NMR data were reduced using unsupervised and supervised feature selection approaches. Multilayer perceptron models were trained using independent training, validation, and test sets. Model performance was evaluated using the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) with 95 percent confidence intervals for clinically (%95CI) relevant liver fat thresholds. Results: A total of 8,091 participants were analyzed. The combined 20 best NMR (dominated by HDL lipid composition and fatty acid profiles, including cholesteryl esters, phospholipids, PUFA/SFA ratios, and selected amino acids) and SteatoTest-2-proxy model demonstrated good discrimination across multiple PDFF-defined thresholds. AUC values were 0.766 (%95CI 0.733–0.800) for S0 vs S1A–S3, 0.766 (0.726–0.806) for S0–S1A vs S1B–S3, and 0.780 (0.668–0.872) for S0– S1B vs S2–S3. Severe steatosis discrimination (S0–S2 vs S3) was 0.884 (0.779–0.957), with limited reliability due to few S3 cases (n = 10). Performance was consistent across sex specific analyses. Conclusion: Deep learning integration of NMR and available NFT biomarkers enables robust blood-based discrimination of PDFFdefined steatosis stages. This multimodal approach supports scalable and noninvasive assessment of steatosis severity in large populations with steatotic liver disease and warrants further validation in cohorts enriched for advanced steatosis.

10.1016/s0168-8278(26)01248-1.title: FRI-569 Using artificial intelligence-based models and radiomics in mri to predict hepatocellular carcinoma after liver transplant
10.1016/s0168-8278(26)01248-1.abstract: Background and aims: Prediction of hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) recurrence after liver transplantation (LT) is essential to personalize surveillance regimen and improve survival post-liver transplant. We aim to utilize AI-based MRI radiomics and clinical metrics to predict HCC recurrence and mortality after LT. Method: A total of 166 patients underwent multi-phase contrastenhanced T1W MRI scans pre-LT at a tertiary center in this retrospective study. Each focal liver lesion was manually contoured by one radiologist and assigned a Liver Imaging Reporting and Data System (LIRADS) score. Patients were classified based on the presence of LIRADS 4 or 5 lesions on their MRIs. Radiomic features were extracted from liver segmentation obtained from an AI model. Radiomic feature selection was performed using the t-test, MannWhitney U test, and the least absolute shrinkage and selection operator. Lesion volume was calculated by summing LIRADS 4 and 5 lesions. Clinical metrics and chosen radiomic features were integrated into univariate (Wilcoxon) and multivariate (Cox proportional hazards) analyses to identify independent predictors of post-LT HCC recurrence and mortality when comparing LIRADS 4 and LIRADS 5 patients. Results: Out of 166 patients, 21 had HCC recurrence, thus resulting in a cumulative incidence rate of 12.7% and a median time to recurrence of about 34 months (IQR: 11.4, 65.5). Two radiomic features were selected for the LIRADS 5 patients, and eight for the LIRADS 4 patients. Two radiomic features (gldm_GrayLevelNonUniformity and shape_MajorAxisLength) overlapped in terms of significance between both patient groups. The Wilcoxon test revealed that liver volume ( p = 0.03) was significantly associated with recurrence 12 months post-LT. In the multivariate analysis adjusted for age and gender, two radiomics features (gldm_DependenceNonUniformity and shape_SurfaceArea) were found to be significant for overall recurrence ( p < 0.05) in LIRADS 5 patients. The same two radiomic features, along with gldm_GrayLevelNonUniformity, were identified as statistically significant ( p < 0.05) for overall mortality in LIRADS 5 patients as well. An additional multivariate analysis, adjusted for age, gender, and tumor volume, indicated that a decrease in liver volume significantly predicts overall recurrence ( p = 0.02) and mortality ( p = 0.03) in LIRADS 5 patients. Conclusion: Utilizing radiomics alongside clinical factors in prediction models may help predict HCC recurrence in LIRADS 5 patients.

10.1016/s0168-8278(26)01682-x.title: WED-140 AI based cell free DNA methylation blood test for semaglutide response in patients with at-risk MASH: Results from SAMARA randomized control trial
10.1016/s0168-8278(26)01682-x.abstract: Background and aims: GLP-1 receptor agonists are emerging as effective treatments for metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH), yet tools to characterize their biological effects remain limited. We analyzed plasma cell-free DNA (cfDNA) methylation from the SAMARA trial to determine whether semaglutide induces distinct epigenetic changes compared to placebo and whether baseline methylation can distinguish treatment responders. Method: Twenty-seven SAMARA participants with paired plasma samples (13 semaglutide, 14 placebo) were analyzed at baseline and end of treatment (∼1 year; dose up to 2.4 mg subcutaneous weekly). A whole-methylome assay and AI model (LiquidTransformer) were used to segment the genome into biologically meaningful units and characterize methylation patterns. For each patient, we computed methylation change (end-of-treatment minus baseline) and identified regions differing between arms using the Mann-Whitney U statistic. Separately, we compared baseline methylation between responders and non-responders within the semaglutide arm. Pathway enrichment analysis was performed on significant regions. Results: Semaglutide-treated patients exhibited methylation trajectories distinct from placebo, demonstrating a treatment-specific biological signal in cfDNA. Pathway analysis identified 28 significantly enriched GO terms: lipid metabolism including cholesterol biosynthesis and fatty acid transport; fibrosis and ECM remodeling including collagen signaling and SMAD regulation; neuronal development including axon guidance and CNS axonogenesis; cardiovascular function including nitric oxide and VEGF signaling; tissue repair including Wnt/catenin signaling; and renal development. Baseline methylation also distinguished responders from non-responders, with enrichment in Wnt/catenin signaling, immune regulation including T cell activation, and tyrosine kinase pathways. Notably, Wnt/catenin was enriched in both analyses, suggesting its role in GLP-1 response biology in MASH. Conclusion: AI-enabled cfDNA methylation profiling distinguished semaglutide from placebo and identified baseline signatures associated with treatment response. Treatment-associated changes independent of clinical response magnitude were present even in partial responders, suggesting cfDNA captures upstream biological effects not yet reflected in clinical outcomes. This approach may support precision strategies for predicting and monitoring GLP-1 agonist response.
